# Post-Repair Inspection Checklist for Intake Leaks

When you discover a breach in your intake hose downstream from the air filter, the immediate instinct is often to patch it with duct tape and move on. While that temporary fix prevents an immediate loss of power or engine code, the system has been operating under compromised conditions for an unknown duration. The critical question isn't just "how do I seal this?" but "what damage did the unfiltered air cause while it was open?"

The most significant risk introduced by a hole in the intake tract is the ingestion of particulate matter. Since the breach occurs downstream of the filter, the engine is now drawing a mixture of filtered and unfiltered air. Depending on how long that leak existed, you could have introduced abrasive debris directly into the intake manifold and the cylinder head ports.

Before you swap in the new hose, you need to assess the condition of the internal components. Do not skip this step if the leak was present for more than a few days. The primary component at risk is the intake manifold itself. Specifically, inspect the plenum chamber and the runners leading to the cylinder heads. Look for visible accumulation of dust or grit that bypassed the filter media. If the engine uses a throttle body downstream of the leak site, that component is also a high-priority inspection target.

### Inspecting the Throttle Body

The throttle body acts as the gatekeeper for airflow into the cylinders. It contains the idle air control valve (IAC) and the butterfly plate. Unfiltered air can leave residue on these surfaces. While some dust may be benign, larger debris or abrasive particles can interfere with the smooth operation of the IAC valve or stick to the throttle plate, causing an uneven idle or rough running conditions once you start the engine with the new hose installed.

The best practice is to remove the throttle body and visually inspect the interior bore. Check the edges of the butterfly plate for scoring or burrs. If the plate spins freely but leaves a trail of black dust on the intake walls, the throttle body likely needs cleaning with an appropriate carburetor cleaner or throttle body cleaner. Do not use harsh abrasives that could damage the sealing surfaces.

### Checking for Secondary Clogging and Vacuum Issues

An intake leak doesn't just introduce dirt; it alters the vacuum profile of the engine. A breach in the hose changes the pressure dynamics upstream and downstream of the hole. When you install the new hose, you must verify that no secondary clogs have formed as a result of the debris migration.

Focus your inspection on the PCV (Positive Crankcase Ventilation) system. If unfiltered air is being sucked into the intake manifold through the leak, it can disrupt the balance of the crankcase ventilation system. Check the PCV valve and its associated hoses for restriction or blockage. A clogged PCV system can lead to sludge buildup on valve stems or excessive oil consumption in the long run.

Additionally, inspect all other vacuum lines connected to the intake manifold. These often run alongside the damaged hose. If debris was sucked into the manifold, it could have migrated into smaller diameter vacuum lines that feed sensors like the MAP (Manifold Absolute Pressure) sensor or EGR valve. Disconnect these lines and blow through them gently to ensure they are not partially blocked by particulate matter.

### Cleaning and Reassembly Protocol

Once you have confirmed the internal condition, cleaning is mandatory before reassembly. Do not simply reinstall the new hose if the throttle body or intake walls are dirty. Use a vacuum cleaner with a narrow nozzle to remove loose debris from the plenum chamber. Follow this with a targeted cleaning of the throttle body.

If you find significant debris that cannot be removed easily, consider whether the cost of cleaning outweighs the risk of keeping the manifold. In some cases, replacing the intake gaskets is a prudent trade-off to ensure a proper seal and prevent future leaks, even if the primary damage is cosmetic. The goal is to restore the system to a state where no unfiltered air or debris can compromise engine performance.

Finally, after reassembly, perform a visual leak check before starting the engine. Use a propane torch or carb spray around the new connections while the engine idles to ensure the repair holds and that there are no lingering vacuum leaks elsewhere in the tract.
